The party ended at a time that didn't belong to either side of the building — not quite the neighborhood's bedtime, not yet the host's. I walked out with the third person, the fourth, and finally alone into the October dark that had been waiting like a patient dog along the curb.

The streetlight on the corner flickered, which meant it was dying for weeks and had finally chosen this Tuesday. I didn't stop to check. There's a particular honesty to being the last one out — the evening still clinging to your coat like lint, someone else's perfume lodged in your hair, your phone buzzing in a way that feels intrusive, like it's still remembering the party while you're already leaving it.

You walk at the speed your body chooses, slower than you think, faster than you think. The air comes in sharp and clean after the heated room. Your breath makes small invisible ghosts. You're not thinking about anything specifically. The party's noise is still in your molars, in the hollow behind your eyes, but the actual content — who said what, which glass you held, the shape of the argument you overheard — is already dissolving, becoming less memory than atmosphere.

You turn into your street. Your own door. The deadbolt with its satisfied clunk. The kitchen dark. You put the kettle on because your hands need something to do, and while the water heats, you stand there in your coat, feeling like a ghost who's forgotten which house is his.
